analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicaid to cover help at home so disabled and older people can avoid nursing homes.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 18 bipartisan cosponsors but never got a vote: referred to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2003, it died there when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicaid currently guarantees only one kind of long-term care in every state: a nursing home. This bill would have required every state's Medicaid program to also cover trained attendant services—help with dressing, bathing, meals, and daily tasks—at home or in the community, for anyone eligible for nursing-home-level care who chooses it. It offered states extra federal money for moving early, grants to reorganize their systems, and required states to design the program with disabled people at the table.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicaid beneficiaries with disabilities and older Americans who need nursing-facility-level care but would rather live at home, with family, or in their communities. The bill's own findings note that only about 27% of Medicaid long-term care dollars go to home and community settings, and home-based care is unevenly available across states [S3]. Family caregivers and home care workers also benefit: grants could fund training and better pay and career prospects for attendant workers [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Makes community-based attendant services a mandatory Medicaid benefit statewide for anyone who qualifies for nursing home or intermediate care facility level care and chooses it, effective by October 2007 [S2][S3].

The bill finds that Medicaid has a funding bias toward institutions: only about 27% of long-term care funds pay for home and community-based care, and nursing home care is the only long-term care service federally guaranteed in every state [S3].

Offers early-adopting states an enhanced federal matching rate plus up to 10 additional percentage points of federal funding for activities like one-stop intake, institutional diversion, family support, and improving attendant workers' earnings and career prospects [S2][S3].
Authorizes $50 million a year in grants (2004-2006) for states to reorganize long-term care around consumer choice, with a Consumer Task Force that must be majority people with disabilities [S2][S3].
Covers one-time transition costs such as rent and utility deposits, bedding, and kitchen supplies when someone moves out of a nursing facility into a community home [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal and state Medicaid budgets, since a new mandatory benefit adds spending, though enhanced federal matching was designed to offset much of it. Nursing facilities would face losing some of the patients and revenue they currently receive by default, since institutional care is the only federally guaranteed option today.

drawbacks.text: A new mandatory Medicaid entitlement increases federal and state spending, and states would have to cover it statewide by a fixed deadline regardless of budget conditions; the enhanced federal match runs only through 2007, after which states bear a larger share [S3].

States and fiscal conservatives could object that the federal government is dictating a new benefit to state Medicaid programs; the bill requires plan amendments and maintenance-of-effort commitments that limit state flexibility [S3].

Shifting care from regulated facilities to private homes raises oversight challenges; the bill responds with quality-assurance, abuse reporting, and monitoring requirements, but policing care delivered in thousands of private residences is harder than in institutions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a widely documented inequity—federal law guarantees institutional care everywhere but home care nowhere—while including real cost controls: consumer direction, maintenance-of-effort rules, quality assurance, and a demonstration project to study costs before broader expansion. The main honest objection is fiscal: a mandatory national benefit with a deadline is expensive, and the enhanced federal match is temporary. The tradeoff is real money versus giving people any choice at all about where they live.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Finance Committee, which handles all Medicaid legislation, never acted on the bill after referring it there in May 2003, and it expired when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 1, 2003 by Sen. Harkin with 11 original cosponsors including two Republicans, and read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1][S5].
It gathered 18 additional cosponsors—3 Republicans and 15 Democrats—but the action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote after the referral [S4][S5].
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 with the bill still in the Finance Committee, so it died and would have had to be reintroduced from scratch [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The nursing facility industry kept the status quo, in which institutional care is the only long-term service Medicaid must cover in every state. Disabled and older Medicaid beneficiaries gained nothing; the institutional funding bias the bill described remained in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing facilities and the Medicaid status quo

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it with remarks in the Senate, framing it as equal access to community-based care for people with disabilities and older Americans [S1][S5].

for.name: 18 of 100 Senators
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan support, but the bill never reached a vote where that support could be tested [S4].

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over Medicaid, chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 1, 2003 and took no further action—no hearing, no markup, no vote—before the Congress expired [S5].

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled action on it; the bill sat for the rest of the 108th Congress [S5].

against.name: Nursing facility industry
against.role: Long-term care institutions whose Medicaid revenue depends on institutional care being the default
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the legislation during its repeated congressional introductions, arguing community-coverage mandates were unfunded and would strain state budgets.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: the bill's 18 cosponsors included 3 Republicans and 15 Democrats, and the original introduction included Republican Sens. Specter and Cochran [S4][S3].

industries.industry: Nursing facilities and intermediate care institutions
industries.note: Federal Medicaid law guarantees nursing home care in every state but not home care, giving institutions a locked-in revenue stream from people who have no alternative. The bill makes home and community care an equal entitlement, letting beneficiaries take their Medicaid dollars elsewhere.

industries.industry: Home care and attendant service agencies
industries.note: A mandatory Medicaid benefit for community-based attendant services creates a large new customer base, and the bill allows agency-provider models alongside consumer-directed ones. Its interests run alongside beneficiaries' need for home-based help.

States gain an enhanced federal match for early adoption and grants, but must add a mandatory statewide benefit by 2007 with maintenance-of-effort commitments. The enhanced match expires in 2007, leaving states with a larger ongoing share.
